name: Lichen Planopilaris
seoTitle: Lichen Planopilaris: Signs, Causes, Treatment | Nina Ross
description: Lichen planopilaris often burns or stings before a patch shows. How we tell it from CCCA at 200x, and how we calm the active margin. Sandy Springs, GA.
subtitle: An inflammatory scarring alopecia that often burns or stings before it shows.

hero.alt: 200x view of perifollicular scale around individual hairs
hero.caption: Scale hugging the base of each hair, at 200x.

quickAnswer: Lichen planopilaris, or LPP, is an inflammatory condition that attacks the upper part of the hair follicle and replaces it with scar tissue. It often announces itself with burning, stinging or itching before there is any visible patch. On the scalp you may see redness and scale hugging the base of individual hairs, small irregular patches rather than one round area, and hairs that lift out easily at the edge of a patch. Like other scarring alopecias, follicles already lost to scar will not regrow, so the goal is stopping the active inflammation and protecting the hair around it. We read your scalp at 200x at Nina Ross Atlanta in Sandy Springs. Serving all of Metro Atlanta.
takeaways: It often burns before it shows.
Calming the active margin protects what's left.

symptoms.title: Symptoms in your words, and ours

items.why: In LPP, immune activity at the upper part of the follicle is commonly linked to burning, stinging or itching. It often starts before there is any visible patch, which is why so many people are told nothing looks wrong.
items.check: We read the exact area that burns at 200x, looking for redness and scale at the base of individual hairs. That way we read the spot you feel, not only the spots you can see.

items.you: There is flaking wrapped around single hairs
items.why: Scale that hugs the base of one hair at a time is commonly linked to inflammation at that follicle. It behaves differently from the loose, all-over flaking of a dry or oily scalp.
items.check: Magnification shows whether scale is wrapped around individual hairs or spread across the surface. That difference points toward LPP or toward a surface condition like seborrheic dermatitis.

items.why: A ring of redness around a hair is commonly linked to active inflammation at that follicle. Redness reads differently on deeper skin tones and is regularly missed.
items.check: We read your scalp under magnification instead of judging by surface color, and mark the follicles where inflammation is still active.

items.you: Patches with odd shapes, not circles
items.why: LPP tends to make small irregular patches that can join together over time, rather than one round area. Smooth, round patches are more often linked to alopecia areata.
items.check: We map the borders at 200x and compare the pattern with CCCA, which usually starts at the crown and spreads outward, before anyone names it.

items.you: Hairs come out with a slight tug
items.us: Positive pull test at the active margin
items.why: At the active edge of a patch, inflamed follicles can let go of hairs more easily. That edge is where the condition is still working.
items.check: We find the active margin, photograph the same points, and re-check them at follow-ups so you can see whether the border has stopped moving.

symptoms.lede: Tap the one that sounds like you to see why it happens and how we figure it out.

items.title: Immune activity at the follicle
items.text: The immune system targets the stem cell region of the follicle. Once that region is lost, the follicle cannot rebuild itself.

items.title: Association with lichen planus
items.text: Some people with LPP also have lichen planus on the skin, nails or inside the mouth. Tell us if you have noticed changes there.

items.title: Hormonal and systemic triggers
items.text: A frontal pattern of LPP is described more often around and after menopause.{cite:1} Thyroid conditions are also reported alongside it.{cite:2}

insight.kicker: What we see that others miss
insight.title: How we tell LPP from CCCA at 200x
insight.text: At 200x the two conditions look different, and that distinction changes what we treat first, which is why we look before anyone names it.

care.title: What care looks like here
care.text: Our first job is finding the active margin and calming it. We use trichoscopy to mark where inflammation is still working, use light-based and restorative support to settle it, and re-photograph the same points so you can see whether the border has stopped moving.

treatments.text: Low level light used to calm scalp inflammation and support the growth phase.

Relaxers, braids, locs, weaves and heat. Share your full hair history. It is welcomed, never judged.

faq.q: Is lichen planopilaris the same as CCCA?
faq.a: No. Both scar, but they behave differently. CCCA usually starts at the crown and spreads outward in a circle. LPP tends to make irregular patches with scale and redness right at the base of the hairs, and it often burns.
Follicles already lost to scar will not regrow. The goal is stopping the active inflammation and protecting the hair around it, which is why reading the active margin early matters.

faq.q: Why does my scalp hurt when nothing looks wrong?
faq.a: LPP often announces itself with burning, stinging or itching before there is any visible patch. The inflammation is already working at the follicle, which is why a 200x read of the spot you feel matters.

faq.q: Can I still get my hair done?
faq.a: Yes. Your styling history is welcome information here. We read which areas are active and talk through what is gentlest on them, so you can keep wearing the hair you love.

faq.q: How do you track whether it is working?
faq.a: We re-photograph the same points at 200x at each visit, so you can see whether the border has stopped moving.
